It protects the attempt trail: the arm reads `exc.code` to record which closed `ComposerPlannerCode` ended the attempt (MALFORMED_RESPONSE, RESPONSE_TRUNCATED, the budget-exhaustion set, DECLINED) an unrecognized planner code maps to `ComposerPlannerAttemptOutcome.GUARD_FIRED`, and anything that is not a `PipelinePlannerError` (or a cancellation) maps to `ComposerPlannerAttemptOutcome.INTERNAL_ERROR` with `planner_code=None` - the attempt trail records only that CLOSED outcome vocabulary, never a free-form class name, so a planner failure is never recorded with a code it did not carry. web/composer/pipeline_planner.py:R5:_pla: The flagged pattern is `isinstance(exc, PydanticValidationError)` inside `except ValueError as exc`. The value is an exception instance from `_PlannerTerminalPayload.model_validate` — a library-owned class that subclasses `ValueError`, checked nominally, which is the ADR-032 form for a type we do not parse. It protects feedback selection: only a pydantic error exposes `exc.errors()`, and only that structure can say whether the failure was in `claimed_deferred_intent_ids` (answer with `_deferred_intent_claim_feedback`) or anywhere else (answer with `_canonical_schema_feedback`). In practice `model_validate` delivers only `PydanticValidationError` here: pydantic v2 wraps a field validator's `ValueError` - including the ones `_PlannerTerminalPayload`'s `claimed_deferred_intent_ids` validator raises - into the `ValidationError` it re-raises, so those failures arrive with `errors()` populated under the `claimed_deferred_intent_ids` loc, never as a bare `ValueError`. The isinstance is what licenses calling `.errors()` at all (`PydanticValidationError` subclasses `ValueError`), and the wider `except ValueError` clause stays honest if any non-pydantic `ValueError` from the surrounding expression ever reaches it, routing it to the canonical branch instead of crashing feedback selection. Splitting this into two `except` clauses (`except PydanticValidationError` / `except ValueError`) was considered and rejected: it trades this one R5 for a second R6 silent handler, leaving the finding count unchanged while duplicating the feedback assignment.

web/composer/pipeline_planner.py:R6:_par: The flagged pattern is `except JsonBoundaryError: pass` around `require_bounded_text(content, label="planner text response")`. The value is Tier-3: `content` is the provider's text reply. The handler is not a swallow — it is a classification fall-through, and the control is the `raise PipelinePlannerError("planner response must call a declared tool", code="PROSE_REPLY")` at the end of the same branch, which every path through this handler reaches. An over-bounds text reply cannot be admitted as a decline, so declining to `return message, ()` leaves it in the no-tool-call class, where it draws the same nudge-retry treatment as any other unadmitted prose reply and is converted back to a terminal MALFORMED_RESPONSE by the loop once the nudge budget is spent. Re-raising `JsonBoundaryError` here would be wrong: it would turn ordinary over-long LLM prose into a provider-breakage error and skip the nudge budget entirely.
web/composer/pipeline_planner.py:R6:_pla: The flagged pattern is `except ValueError as exc:` whose body assigns rather than returns, so the rule's `_handler_is_silent` test (no `raise`, no non-default `return`) fires even though the handler has an explicit, audited outcome. The value is Tier-3: the exception comes from `_PlannerTerminalPayload.model_validate(deep_thaw(call.arguments))`, i.e. the model's terminal tool-call arguments failing our own canonical schema. The handler's outcome is `terminal_feedback`, and the controls that consume it are named and unavoidable: `_feedback_error_codes(terminal_feedback)` extracts the closed rejection codes, `trail.finish_attempt(..., "candidate_rejected", codes=...)` writes the rejection into the attempt trail, the feedback is appended to `messages` as the tool reply so the model sees exactly why its candidate was refused, and `repair_count`/`repair_budget` bound the loop — exhaustion raises `_rejection_exhausted()`. A malformed candidate therefore never reaches `finalized_pipeline`; the `if terminal_feedback is None:` gate stands between this handler and every acceptance path. Two restructurings were considered and rejected: returning from a helper (`_validated_terminal_payload`) would clear the finding only by moving it out of sight behind indirection, which this project forbids; splitting into `except PydanticValidationError` / `except ValueError` produces two silent handlers instead of one and leaves the count unchanged.

The flagged pattern is `except asyncio.CancelledError as exc: task_error = exc` around `task.exception()` while draining completed discovery tasks. The exception is not swallowed at all — it is CAPTURED and then raised: the very next statement is `if task_error is not None: primary_error = task_error; break`, and the block below ends in `raise primary_error` after `await asyncio.gather(*discovery_tasks, return_exceptions=True)` has drained every sibling so each dispatch reaches its audit record. `task.exception()` raises rather than returns when the task was cancelled, so this handler is the only way to obtain the real cancellation instance; the alternative, `task_error = asyncio.CancelledError(...) if task.cancelled() else task.exception()`, would FABRICATE an exception object in place of the one the loop actually raised, which is the Tier-1 fabrication this rule set exists to prevent. The control is therefore `raise primary_error` in the same function.
web/composer/pipeline_planner.py:R6:_pro: The flagged pattern is `except TypeError: return None` around `vars(value)`. The value is Tier-3 — an unpinned litellm/provider response object — and this handler is the boundary's declared sentinel path: `_provider_fields` carries an `@observation_boundary` whose recorded invariant is that it returns a field mapping "or None when the value is not a Mapping and has no accessible `__dict__`; never raises". `vars()` is the only way to ask that question, and it answers by raising `TypeError`; the alternatives are strictly worse under this same rule set (`hasattr` is R3, `getattr(value, "__dict__", None)` is R2). The control that makes the sentinel safe is named and one hop away: `_provider_field` is the sole reader and returns `None` for every field when `fields is None`, and each of its call sites in `_parse_response_tool_calls` converts a `None` field into an explicit terminal `raise PipelinePlannerError(..., code="MALFORMED_RESPONSE")` — "planner response must contain exactly one choice", "planner response choice is missing its message". Nothing downstream treats an unreadable provider object as a successful parse.
web/composer/pipeline_planner.py:R7:_awa: The flagged pattern is `with suppress(asyncio.CancelledError): await asyncio.shield(task)` inside the `while not task.done():` drain loop. The value is not external data — this is cancellation control flow around an idempotent custody settlement. The loop re-shields until the settlement task genuinely finishes; each further cancellation delivered while we wait must not abandon the in-flight custody write, which is what this suppression prevents. Both suppressions sit inside an `except asyncio.CancelledError:` arm that ends in a bare `raise`, so the original cancellation is preserved unconditionally — the control is that trailing `raise`, which no path through the handler can skip. On the NORMAL (uncancelled) path the awaited work is not wrapped in any suppression at all: `await asyncio.shield(task)` propagates a settlement/custody failure to the caller exactly as it would without this function. The suppressions therefore change behaviour only while the request task is already being torn down, where re-raising would replace the active `CancelledError` and break asyncio's cancellation contract. Rewriting it as `try/except asyncio.CancelledError: pass` would trade R7 for R6 without changing behaviour.
